package_info.package_versions: All versions supporting native Java serialization
package_info.why_malicious: The Java serialization mechanism is not inherently malicious, but its design allows attackers to craft serialized data streams that can instantiate arbitrary classes and trigger code execution during deserialization. This self-defining protocol, if unguarded, enables attackers to exploit application logic and execute arbitrary code, making any application using untrusted Java serialization streams potentially vulnerable.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream(f));
HelloSerialisedWorld hw = (HelloSerialisedWorld) ois.readObject();
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At deserialization time, the code reads a serialized object stream, instantiates objects as defined in the stream, and assigns them to application variables, potentially triggering code execution in constructors or readObject methods of attacker-controlled classes.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deserializing untrusted data allows attackers to control which classes are instantiated, potentially triggering malicious code in constructors or special deserialization methods.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects only safe, expected classes to be deserialized. Malicious behavior occurs when arbitrary or attacker-controlled classes are instantiated, leading to code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Deserialization of trusted data from known sources is legitimate in many applications.
key_indicators: Deserialization of data from untrusted or user-controlled sources
Lack of class whitelisting or validation during deserialization

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Serialized stream with field value class name: java.lang.Integer (or attacker-controlled class with malicious code in constructor/readObject)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At deserialization time, the code instantiates a class as specified in the serialized stream (e.g., java.lang.Integer or an attacker-supplied class), potentially executing arbitrary code in the process, even if assignment to the target field fails.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The deserialization process instantiates classes based on attacker-controlled input, allowing execution of code in constructors or deserialization hooks before type assignment checks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Expected behavior is to only instantiate safe, expected types. Malicious behavior occurs when arbitrary classes are instantiated, leading to code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use occurs when deserializing trusted data with known, safe types.
key_indicators: Instantiation of classes not expected by the application
Exceptions thrown after instantiation, indicating code was already executed

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a serialized data stream specifying a malicious or unexpected class in a field value.
Application deserializes the crafted stream, instantiating the attacker-controlled class and executing its constructor or deserialization hooks.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution within the application context.

attack_chain.action: Type assignment fails, exception is thrown, but malicious code has already executed.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential masking of attack due to exception, attacker achieves code execution.

behavioral_signatures: Deserialization of untrusted or user-supplied data streams
Instantiation of unexpected or attacker-controlled classes during deserialization
Execution of code in constructors or readObject methods during deserialization
file_indicators: Serialized files with unexpected class names in field values
Serialized streams containing references to classes not present in application logic
network_indicators: Inbound or outbound transfer of serialized Java objects from untrusted sources
Unusual network activity following deserialization events
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for deserialization of data from untrusted sources, especially when using ObjectInputStream or similar APIs. Implement class whitelisting or validation to restrict which classes can be instantiated during deserialization. Analyze serialized data streams for unexpected or unauthorized class references. Alert on exceptions during deserialization that occur after object instantiation, as this may indicate attempted exploitation.
